A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MDOT and PNCG for discrete optimal transport. Their full text, equations, figures and appendices are readable, and corresponding content can be matched despite substantial revision and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendix E report original synthetic optimal-transport experiments and MNIST benchmarks, including convergence, timing and conditioning results.

after.justification: v2 Sections 4.1–4.2 report original warm-start, preconditioning and convergence experiments, together with timing and accuracy benchmarks on upsampled MNIST.

M1.justification: v1 reuses previous dual updates with fixed step sizes and projection thresholds fixed across MD steps. v2 introduces step-size-scaled warm-starts, the two-update MDOT2 variant, and an entropy/temperature-dependent stopping threshold using L1 marginal infeasibility (Equations 17–19). These change the procedure. The Sinkhorn-direction preconditioner, PPR update and hybrid secant/bisection line search remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate discrete optimal transport using synthetic cost matrices and entropy-controlled marginals, plus MNIST images. Upsampling MNIST and changing problem sizes alter preprocessing and evaluation settings without introducing a new population, domain or transport task.

E2.justification: The MNIST comparison retains MDOT-Sinkhorn and Mirror Sinkhorn, while v2 Figure 4 adds separately evaluated log-domain stabilized Sinkhorn and the fast and safe settings of Feydy's Algorithm 3.5. v2 Figure 1 also introduces an explicit epsilon-scaling warm-start comparator. These are evaluated comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: MNIST changes from 28×28 images and 512 pairs to upsampled 64×64 images and 32 pairs. The GPU changes from GTX 1080 to RTX 2080 Ti. Step-size schedules, accuracy sweeps and feasibility criteria are revised. The preconditioning experiment now measures residual error after 500 steps from a controlled initial error, replacing iterations-to-convergence measurements.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparisons of first- and second-order warm-starts against epsilon-scaling under two temperature schedules. It substantially revises the entropy/preconditioning and projection-convergence analyses, replacing v1's fixed-T sweeps and per-MD-step convergence plots. Problem-size sensitivity is retained in revised form in v2 Figure 3; it already appeared in v1 Appendix E.

E5.justification: Repeated sampling and uncertainty reporting already exist in v1. v2 changes means to medians and reports 80% and 60% intervals for synthetic analyses, whereas v1 Figure 2 specifies one-standard-deviation shading. Reported synthetic sample/run counts change from 32 to 20, 30 or 16. MNIST retains nominal 90% intervals but uses 32 rather than 512 pairs.

E6.justification: The numerical evidence is substantially replaced and extended. v2 Figure 1 reports roughly 3–4× fewer Sinkhorn iterations than epsilon-scaling under slow temperature decay. Figure 4 reports stabilized Sinkhorn taking about 10× MDOT-PNCG's time at relative error 10^-6, while neither Feydy setting reaches below 1% error. These are new results under revised settings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v1's Corollary 3.4 bounding consecutive transport-plan distances and its Pinsker-based proof are removed. v2 adds Taylor and backward finite-difference derivations for warm-starting, including Appendix B.1, and mathematical justification for adaptive projection accuracy. The main exact-MD error bounds, entropic equivalence result and Sinkhorn contraction proposition are retained.

C1.justification: The central claims about MDOT/PNCG, high-precision computation and advantages for high-entropy marginals remain. v2 refines the contribution around improved epsilon-scaling warm-starts, quantifies the abstract's precision claim at relative error 10^-8, and explicitly frames performance against stabilized Sinkhorn and recent solvers on higher-dimensional problems.

C2.justification: v2 develops the interpretation that intermediate projections primarily support warm-starting, motivating reduced effort at high temperatures. It adds explanations for Feydy's accumulated projection errors and MSK's slowing convergence, and qualifies debiased distance estimates as not providing feasible transport plans. These materially expand the mechanism and applicability discussion beyond v1's retained entropy/conditioning interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 documents LogSumExp-based computations, reuse of marginal sums during line search, and optional PyKeOps/CUDA cost evaluation with O(n) storage. It explicitly states that rounding time is excluded from timing measurements. Conversely, the explicit repository link supplied in v1 is absent from v2. These are changes in documented implementation and access information.

R1.justification: Beyond moving related work into the main text, v2 substantially reframes MDOT relative to epsilon-scaling, Schmitzer's work and Feydy's solver. It adds discussion of multiscale and curvature-aware approaches and broader application literature. Much of v1's linear-programming/minimum-cost-flow survey and associated complexity discussion is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Warm-starting and stopping criteria receive separate subsections; related work moves from Appendix D to main Section 5; data-generation details move into the new Appendix D. This is substantial narrative reorganization beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v1's conceptual Figure 1 is removed. The experimental displays are extensively redesigned, including dual-axis warm-start plots, revised conditioning axes, replacement of six-panel ablation displays, and an expanded MNIST legend and changed uncertainty presentation. The appendix size analysis is reformulated in a main-text figure, and algorithm boxes change from embedded to full-width layouts.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1's practical validation by directly comparing with stabilized Sinkhorn and epsilon-scaling, while clarifying the specific warm-start contribution relative to prior approaches. The controlled comparisons and explicit stopping-rule rationale substantially strengthen the paper's support and positioning. Smaller MNIST samples, removed fixed-T analyses and loss of the repository link are drawbacks, but the stronger comparative foundation and methodological explanation provide a clear overall gain.
